claim: Canonical transient receptor potential channels (TRPC) are involved in receptor-operated and/or store-operated Ca2+ signaling.
source: Canonical transient receptor potential channels (TRPC) are involved in receptor-operated and/or store-operated Ca2+ signaling.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that establishes the general function of TRPC channels, supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Inhibition of TRPCs by small molecules was shown to be promising in treating renal diseases.
source: Inhibition of TRPCs by small molecules was shown to be promising in treating renal diseases.
evidence: This statement references prior research findings about therapeutic applications, implicitly citing previous work.

claim: In cells, TRPC channels are regulated by calmodulin (CaM).
source: In cells, the channels are regulated by calmodulin (CaM).
evidence: This is a known regulatory mechanism supported by established scientific knowledge and citations in the manuscript.

claim: All three pyridazinone-based inhibitors bind to the same cavity of the voltage-sensing-like domain of TRPC4.
source: The structures reveal that all the inhibitors bind to the same cavity of the voltage-sensing-like domain and allow us to describe how structural changes from the ligand-binding site can be transmitted to the central ion-conducting pore of TRPC4.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by structural data from cryo-EM experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: CaM binds to the rib helix of TRPC4.
source: CaM binds to the rib helix of TRPC4, which results in the ordering of a previously disordered region, fixing the channel in its closed conformation.
evidence: This is supported by structural data from the TRPC4-CaM complex structure determined in this study.

claim: CaM binding to TRPC4 results in the ordering of a previously disordered region.
source: CaM binds to the rib helix of TRPC4, which results in the ordering of a previously disordered region, fixing the channel in its closed conformation.
evidence: This is directly observed in the structural comparison between apo and CaM-bound TRPC4 structures.

claim: CaM binding fixes TRPC4 in its closed conformation.
source: CaM binds to the rib helix of TRPC4, which results in the ordering of a previously disordered region, fixing the channel in its closed conformation.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis showing the channel remains closed upon CaM binding.

claim: The CaM-induced regulatory mechanism of TRPC4 represents a novel mechanism for canonical TRP channels.
source: This represents a novel CaM-induced regulatory mechanism of canonical TRP channels.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with other TRP channel regulatory mechanisms and the unique binding mode observed.

claim: TRP ion channels mediate nociception, mechanosensation and store-operated Ca2+ signaling.
source: Transient receptor potential (TRP) ion channels mediate a plethora of vital cellular functions, including nociception, mechanosensation and store-operated Ca2+ signaling (Clapham, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Clapham, 2003.

claim: TRPC channels are involved in neuronal development and plasticity, vasorelaxation and kidney dysfunction.
source: Members belonging to the canonical TRP subfamily (TRPC) are involved in neuronal development and plasticity, as well as in vasorelaxation and kidney dysfunction (Hall et al., 2019; Kochukov et al., 2013; Phelan et al., 2013; Riccio et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to Hall et al., 2019; Kochukov et al., 2013; Phelan et al., 2013; Riccio et al., 2009.

claim: Malfunction of TRPC channels is linked to neurological disorders and cardiac hypertrophy.
source: As a result, malfunction is often linked to pathologies such as neurological disorders and cardiac hypertrophy (Selvaraj et al., 2010; Wu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Selvaraj et al., 2010; Wu et al., 2010.

claim: TRPC4 and TRPC5 share 70% sequence identity.
source: Within the TRPC1/4/5 sub-group, TRPC4 and TRPC5 share the highest sequence identity of 70% (Plant and Schaefer, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Plant and Schaefer, 2003.

claim: TRPC4 and TRPC5 can form homo-tetrameric channels that allow the passage of Ca2+ and Na+ ions.
source: Both proteins can form homo-tetrameric channels that allow the passage of Ca2+, but also Na+ ions to a lesser extent (Minard et al., 2018; Owsianik et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Minard et al., 2018; Owsianik et al., 2006.

claim: TRPC1 shares approximately 48% identity with TRPC4/5.
source: In contrast, TRPC1, which shares approximately 48% identity with TRPC4/5, rather participates in the formation of hetero-tetrameric TRPC1/4/5 channels (Bröker-Lai et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bröker-Lai et al., 2017.

claim: TRPC1 participates in the formation of hetero-tetrameric TRPC1/4/5 channels.
source: In contrast, TRPC1, which shares approximately 48% identity with TRPC4/5, rather participates in the formation of hetero-tetrameric TRPC1/4/5 channels (Bröker-Lai et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bröker-Lai et al., 2017.

claim: TRPC4 is widely expressed in tissues associated with the nervous, cardiovascular, and immune systems.
source: TRPC4 is widely expressed in various tissues associated with the nervous-, cardiovascular- and immune system (Freichel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Freichel et al., 2014.

claim: TRPC4 is necessary for neurite outgrowth.
source: It has been shown to be necessary for neurite outgrowth, and its expression is upregulated in axonal regeneration after nerve injury (Wu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wu et al., 2008.

claim: TRPC4 expression is upregulated in axonal regeneration after nerve injury.
source: It has been shown to be necessary for neurite outgrowth, and its expression is upregulated in axonal regeneration after nerve injury (Wu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wu et al., 2008.

claim: TRPC4 is regulated by the ER-resident calcium sensor Stim1.
source: TRPC4 was shown to be regulated by the ER-resident calcium sensor Stim1, the lipid-binding protein SESTD1 and the G-protein Gαi2 (Jeon et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2010; Miehe et al., 2010; Zeng et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jeon et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2010; Miehe et al., 2010; Zeng et al., 2008.

claim: TRPC4 is regulated by the lipid-binding protein SESTD1.
source: TRPC4 was shown to be regulated by the ER-resident calcium sensor Stim1, the lipid-binding protein SESTD1 and the G-protein Gαi2 (Jeon et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2010; Miehe et al., 2010; Zeng et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jeon et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2010; Miehe et al., 2010; Zeng et al., 2008.

claim: TRPC4 is regulated by the G-protein Gαi2.
source: TRPC4 was shown to be regulated by the ER-resident calcium sensor Stim1, the lipid-binding protein SESTD1 and the G-protein Gαi2 (Jeon et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2010; Miehe et al., 2010; Zeng et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jeon et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2010; Miehe et al., 2010; Zeng et al., 2008.

claim: TRPC4 was proposed to act as a receptor-operated channel (ROC).
source: Dependent on the respective cellular environment in combination with the experimental method used for the measurement, TRPC4 was proposed to either act as a receptor-operated channel (ROC) (Schaefer et al., 2000; Schaefer et al., 2002) or as a store-operated channel (SOC) (Wang et al., 2004; Warnat et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schaefer et al., 2000; Schaefer et al., 2002.

claim: TRPC4 was proposed to act as a store-operated channel (SOC).
source: Dependent on the respective cellular environment in combination with the experimental method used for the measurement, TRPC4 was proposed to either act as a receptor-operated channel (ROC) (Schaefer et al., 2000; Schaefer et al., 2002) or as a store-operated channel (SOC) (Wang et al., 2004; Warnat et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2004; Warnat et al., 1999.

claim: Calmodulin (CaM) and inositol 1,4,5-triphosphate receptor (IP3R) compete for the same binding site on TRPC4.
source: In the studies, describing TRPC4 as SOC, two key proteins, calmodulin (CaM) and inositol 1,4,5-triphosphate receptor (IP3R), compete for the same binding site on TRPC4 (Mery et al., 2001; Tang et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mery et al., 2001; Tang et al., 2001.

claim: Ca2+-dependent binding of CaM inhibits TRPC4 in the resting state.
source: First, Ca2+-dependent binding of CaM inhibits the channel in the resting state.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and citations in the manuscript.

claim: When intracellular Ca2+ levels decrease, IP3 receptor interacts with TRPC4, displacing CaM, to restore channel activity.
source: When intracellular Ca2+ levels decrease, the activating IP3 receptor directly interacts with TRPC4, displacing CaM, to restore channel activity (Kanki et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kanki et al., 2001.

claim: As a receptor-operated channel, TRPC4 is activated by Gαi2 coupled to the phospholipase C (PLC) signaling pathway.
source: As ROC, the channel is activated by Gαi2 coupled to the phospholipase C (PLC) signaling pathway (Schaefer et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Schaefer et al., 2000.

claim: DAG directly binds to and activates TRPC4 and TRPC5.
source: Specifically, the secondary messenger DAG, which is released upon the hydrolysis of phosphatidylinositol-4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) by PLC, directly binds to and activates TRPC4 and TRPC5 (Mederos y Schnitzler et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mederos y Schnitzler et al., 2018.

claim: (-)-Englerin A (EA) shows high potency and selectivity for TRPC4/5.
source: Activation of channels by the natural compound (-)-Englerin A (EA), which shows high potency and selectivity for TRPC4/5, inhibits tumor growth of renal cancer cells through increased Ca2+ influx (Akbulut et al., 2015; Carson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Akbulut et al., 2015; Carson et al., 2015.

claim: (-)-Englerin A inhibits tumor growth of renal cancer cells through increased Ca2+ influx.
source: Activation of channels by the natural compound (-)-Englerin A (EA), which shows high potency and selectivity for TRPC4/5, inhibits tumor growth of renal cancer cells through increased Ca2+ influx (Akbulut et al., 2015; Carson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Akbulut et al., 2015; Carson et al., 2015.

claim: Riluzole, BTD and methylprednisolone are activators of TRPC4/5.
source: Other activators include riluzole, BTD and the glucocorticoid methylprednisolone (Beckmann et al., 2017; Richter et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Beckmann et al., 2017; Richter et al., 2014.

claim: Inhibitors of TRPC4/5 are mostly used to target renal diseases such as focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS).
source: Inhibitors of TRPC4/5 are mostly used to target renal diseases such as focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) (Mundel et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2017), but can also have a therapeutic effect on the central nervous system (CNS) (Just et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mundel et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2017.

claim: TRPC4/5 inhibitors can have a therapeutic effect on the central nervous system (CNS).
source: Inhibitors of TRPC4/5 are mostly used to target renal diseases such as focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) (Mundel et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2017), but can also have a therapeutic effect on the central nervous system (CNS) (Just et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Just et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2015.

claim: Two TRPC4/5 inhibitor compounds are in clinical trials for treating proteinuric kidney disease and anxiety disorder/depression.
source: Currently, two compounds are in clinical trials aiming to treat a proteinuric kidney disease and anxiety disorder/depression, conducted by Goldfinch Bio (NCT03970122) and Hydra/Boehringer Ingelheim (NCT03210272), respectively (Mundel et al., 2019; Wulff et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mundel et al., 2019; Wulff et al., 2019 and clinical trial identifiers.

claim: Xanthine-based inhibitors HC-070 and HC-608 have exceptional high potency for TRPC1/4/5 but suffer from poor physiochemical properties such as low solubility.
source: While xanthine-based inhibitors, such as HC-070 and HC-608 (formerly known as Pico145) have assisted in advancing the field of pharmacological modulation of TRPC1/4/5 due to their exceptional high potency, they suffer from poor physiochemical properties such as low solubility (Just et al., 2018; Rubaiy et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Just et al., 2018; Rubaiy et al., 2017.

claim: A novel class of small molecule modulators selective for TRPC4/5 was identified in a high-throughput screen, building on a piperazinone/pyridazinone scaffold.
source: Recently, a novel class of small molecule modulators selective for TRPC4/5 was identified in a high-throughput screen, building up on a piperazinone/pyridazinone scaffold (Yu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yu et al., 2019.

claim: GFB-8438 showed promise as a potential drug for the treatment of proteinuric kidney disease, exhibiting favorable in vitro and in vivo properties.
source: In particular, GFB-8438 showed promise as a potential drug for the treatment of proteinuric kidney disease, exhibiting overall favorable in vitro and in vivo properties (Yu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yu et al., 2019.

claim: In vitro, mouse podocytes were protected from protamine-induced injury when treated with GFB-8438.
source: In vitro, mouse podocytes were protected from protamine-induced injury when treated with the inhibitor.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yu et al., 2019 in the preceding sentence.

claim: GFB-8438 demonstrated robust efficacy in a hypertensive deoxycorticosterone acetate (DOCA)-salt rat model of FSGS, reducing albumin concentration and total protein levels.
source: Importantly, GFB-8438 also demonstrated robust efficacy in a hypertensive deoxycorticosterone acetate (DOCA)-salt rat model of FSGS, in which both albumin concentration and total protein levels were significantly reduced (Yu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yu et al., 2019.

claim: Structures of TRPC6 in complex with the activator AM-0883 and the inhibitor AM-1473 have been reported.
source: The structures of TRPC6 in complex with the activator AM-0883 and the inhibitor AM-1473 have been reported recently (Bai et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bai et al., 2020.

claim: Structures of TRPC5 in complex with the inhibitors clemizole, HC-070 and Pico145 have been reported by two different groups.
source: Following this study, the structures of TRPC5 in complex with the inhibitors clemizole, HC-070 and Pico145 have been reported by two different groups (Song et al., 2020; Wright et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Song et al., 2020; Wright et al., 2020.

claim: Small molecules bind at the voltage-sensor-like (VSL) domain or at the lipid-binding pocket situated close to the pore region in TRPC5.
source: These structures show that the small molecules bind at the voltage-sensor-like (VSL) domain or at the lipid-binding pocket situated close to the pore region.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Song et al., 2020; Wright et al., 2020 in the preceding sentence.

claim: Perfusion of TRPC4-expressing Xenopus oocytes with (-)-Englerin A (0.1 or 1 µM) induced large inward currents at –40 mV.
source: Expectedly, perfusion of the oocytes with the known activator (-)-Englerin A (0.1 or 1 µM) induced large inward currents at –40 mV.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data from two-electrode voltage clamp experiments.

claim: Perfusing TRPC4-expressing oocytes with GFB-9289, GFB-8438 or GFB-8749 did not induce any current change.
source: However, perfusing the oocytes with increasing doses of GFB-9289, GFB-8438 or GFB-8749 did not induce any current change, even in inside-out excised patches from oocytes or in TRPC4-expressing HEK293 cells (data not shown).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data from electrophysiology experiments.

claim: GFB-9289, GFB-8438 and GFB-8749 inhibited (-)-Englerin A activation in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Instead, GFB-9289, GFB-8438 and GFB-8749 inhibited (-)-Englerin A activation in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 1A–C,E–G and I–K).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: (-)-Englerin A and the pyridazinone-based compounds are competitive antagonists.
source: Moreover, competition assays clearly showed that (-)-Englerin A and the respective compounds are competitive antagonists, although we cannot determine if they compete for the same binding site (Figure 1D,H and L).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data from competition assays shown in Figure 1.

claim: The structure of GFB-8438-bound TRPC4 was determined to an average resolution of 3.6 Å.
source: Using cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) and single particle analysis, we have determined the structures of GFB-8438, GFB-9289 and GFB-8749-bound TRPC4 to an average resolution of 3.6 Å, 3.2 Å, and 3.8 Å respectively (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This is directly supported by cryo-EM data and resolution determination.

claim: The structure of GFB-9289-bound TRPC4 was determined to an average resolution of 3.2 Å.
source: Using cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) and single particle analysis, we have determined the structures of GFB-8438, GFB-9289 and GFB-8749-bound TRPC4 to an average resolution of 3.6 Å, 3.2 Å, and 3.8 Å respectively (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This is directly supported by cryo-EM data and resolution determination.

claim: The structure of GFB-8749-bound TRPC4 was determined to an average resolution of 3.8 Å.
source: Using cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) and single particle analysis, we have determined the structures of GFB-8438, GFB-9289 and GFB-8749-bound TRPC4 to an average resolution of 3.6 Å, 3.2 Å, and 3.8 Å respectively (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This is directly supported by cryo-EM data and resolution determination.

claim: The structures of inhibitor-bound TRPC4 complexes are similar to the previously determined TRPC4 apo structure.
source: Overall, the structures of these complexes are similar to the previously determined TRPC4 apo structure (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 4).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison data.

claim: GFB-8438 binds inside a cavity formed by the VSL domain, TRP helix and re-entrant loop.
source: In the GFB-8438-bound structure, we found an additional density compared to the apo structure inside a cavity formed by the VSL domain, TRP helix and re-entrant loop (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM density map.

claim: The nitrogen, chlorine, and oxo group of the pyridazinone ring of GFB-8438 form hydrogen bonds and halogen bonds with N442, Y373, and S488 of TRPC4.
source: The nitrogen, the chlorine, and the oxo group of the pyridazinone ring form hydrogen bonds as well as halogen bonds with N442 of helix S3, Y373 of helix S1 and S488 of the S4 helix, respectively.
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure and supported by the cryo-EM density.

claim: The hydrophobic part of the pyridazinone ring of GFB-8438 is stabilized by a π-π stacking interaction with F413 and M441.
source: The hydrophobic part of the pyridazinone ring is stabilized by a π-π stacking interaction with F413 of helix S2 on one side and M441 of helix S3 on the opposite side.
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure.

claim: The residues interacting with GFB-8438 are identical between TRPC4 and TRPC5.
source: The residues interacting with the inhibitor are identical between TRPC4 and TRPC5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) indicating a similar ligand binding mode in TRPC5, which is supported by their close IC50 values of 0.18 and 0.29 μM for human TRPC5 and human TRPC4, respectively (Yu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data and IC50 values from Yu et al., 2019.

claim: The IC50 values of GFB-8438 are 0.18 μM for human TRPC5 and 0.29 μM for human TRPC4.
source: The residues interacting with the inhibitor are identical between TRPC4 and TRPC5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) indicating a similar ligand binding mode in TRPC5, which is supported by their close IC50 values of 0.18 and 0.29 μM for human TRPC5 and human TRPC4, respectively (Yu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yu et al., 2019.

claim: GFB-9289 binds to the same region as GFB-8438 in TRPC4.
source: Given the common chemical scaffold structure with the difference limited to one part of the molecule, it is not surprising that they bind to the same region.
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM structures.

claim: The reduced size of the cyclohexyl group in GFB-9289 results in the reorientation of interacting residues Y646 and H369.
source: The reduced size of the cyclohexyl group results in the reorientation of interacting residues. Importantly, Y646 of the TRP helix and H369 of the S2 helix do not interact with the compound and are rotating away from the interface (Figure 3B C).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure by comparing GFB-9289 and GFB-8438 binding.

claim: The reduced stabilization of GFB-9289 is the likely cause for weaker binding compared to GFB-8438.
source: This reduced stabilization of GFB-9289 is the likely cause for the weaker binding in comparison to the GFB-8438 (Figure 1).
evidence: This is inferred from structural observations and electrophysiology data.

claim: GFB-8749 shares a common scaffold with GFB-8438 and GFB-9289.
source: The structure of GFB-8749 shares a common scaffold with GFB-8438 and GFB-9289, consisting of three six-membered rings.
evidence: This is directly observed in the chemical structures.

claim: The interaction of protein residues with the pyridazinone ring and piperazinone ring of GFB-8749 are almost identical to those of GFB-8438 and GFB-9289.
source: Thus, the interaction of the protein residues with the pyridazinone ring and 1,4-disubstituted piperazinone ring are found to be almost identical with that of GFB-8438 and GFB-9289 (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structures.

claim: All pyridazinone-based compounds target the VSL domain of TRPC4/5 to modulate channel activity.
source: Given the similar structure of all the three compounds, it is intriguing to suggest that all pyridazinone-based compounds target the VSL domain of TRPC4/5 to modulate the activity of the channel.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data showing all three compounds bind to the same site.

claim: In the apo structure, some residues of the ligand binding pocket interact with each other via hydrophobic and hydrophilic interactions.
source: In the apo structure, some of the residues of the ligand binding pocket interact with each other via hydrophobic (Y373, F413, M441) and hydrophilic interactions (R491 and E438) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the apo structure.

claim: Upon ligand binding, residues in the binding pocket move and reshape to accommodate the ligands, indicating an induced-fit mechanism or conformational selection.
source: Upon ligand binding, these residues move and reshape the pocket to accommodate the ligands, indicating an induced-fit mechanism or conformational selection (Hammes et al., 2009; Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This is inferred from structural comparison and supported by citation to Hammes et al., 2009.

claim: GFB-8438 is more specific for TRPC4/5 than TRPC6.
source: The inhibitor GFB-8438 has been shown to be more specific for TRPC4/5 than TRPC6 (Yu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yu et al., 2019.

claim: N442 in TRPC4/5 is replaced by L534 in TRPC6, which abrogates hydrogen bond formation with the nitrogen atom of pyridazinone.
source: The cognate N442 residue in TRPC4/5 is replaced by L534 in TRPC6, which abrogates hydrogen bond formation with the nitrogen atom of pyridazinone.
evidence: This is directly observed by comparing the structures and sequences of TRPC4/5 and TRPC6.

claim: F413 in TRPC4 is replaced by M505 in TRPC6, reducing interaction with the pyridazinone ring.
source: F413, which in TRPC4 forms a π-π interaction with the pyridazinone ring, is replaced by the weakly interacting hydrophobic residue M505 in TRPC6 (Figure 3E F).
evidence: This is directly observed by comparing the structures of TRPC4 and TRPC6.

claim: The substitutions in the ligand binding pocket explain the much lower binding affinity of TRPC6 for GFB-8438 (>30 μM).
source: These crucial substitutions in the ligand binding pocket explain the much lower binding affinity of TRPC6 for GFB-8438 (>30 μM) (Yu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is inferred from structural observations and supported by binding affinity data from Yu et al., 2019.

claim: GFB-8438 and GFB-8749 interact with both the TRP helix and the VSL domain, whereas GFB-9289 exclusively interacts with the VSL domain.
source: Interestingly, we have observed that the inhibitors GFB-8438 and GFB-8749, which have lower IC50 values than GFB-9289, interact with both the TRP helix and the VSL domain, whereas GFB-9289 exclusively interacts with the VSL domain (Figures 1, 3G).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structures.

claim: Interaction of inhibitors with the peripheral VSL domain is mainly responsible for the allosteric inhibition of TRPC4.
source: This suggests that interaction of the compounds with the peripheral VSL domain is mainly responsible for the allosteric inhibition of the channel, and additional interaction of the inhibitor with the TRP helix amplifies this effect.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural and functional data.

claim: Additional interaction of the inhibitor with the TRP helix amplifies the inhibitory effect.
source: This suggests that interaction of the compounds with the peripheral VSL domain is mainly responsible for the allosteric inhibition of the channel, and additional interaction of the inhibitor with the TRP helix amplifies this effect.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the IC50 values and binding modes of the three inhibitors.

claim: Direct stabilizing interaction with the TRP helix constrains it and the adjacent S6 helix, arresting the channel in a closed state.
source: We hypothesize that the direct stabilizing interaction with the TRP helix constrains it and the adjacent S6 helix thereby arresting the channel in a closed state.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural observations.

claim: The VSL domain acts as a regulatory region in TRP channels in general.
source: Inhibitors were also shown to bind to the VSL domain in other TRP family members (Bai et al., 2020; Diver et al., 2019; Singh et al., 2018b), indicating that this domain acts in general as a regulatory region in TRP channels (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with other TRP channel structures and supported by citations.

claim: Besides GFB-9289, all VSL-bound inhibitors interact with both the VSL domain and the TRP helix.
source: Interestingly, besides GFB-9289, all VSL-bound inhibitors not only interact with the VSL domain but also with the TRP helix.
evidence: This is observed by comparing structures of different TRP channels with bound inhibitors.

claim: The channel is closed at the lower gate in all structures of the inhibitor-bound TRPC4.
source: Similar to the apo structure, the channel is closed at the lower gate in all structures of the inhibitor-bound TRPC4.
evidence: This is directly observed in the structures.

claim: The lower gate shows a minimal constriction defined by residue N621 with a van der Waals surface diameter of approximately 0.7 Å.
source: The lower gate shows a minimal constriction defined by residue N621 with a van der Waals surface diameter of approximately 0.7 Å, which is too narrow for Ca2+ to pass through (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is directly measured from the structures using pore radius calculations.

claim: The backbone residues F576 and G577 forming the TRPC4 selectivity filter show a slightly wider radius in the ligand-bound structures compared to the apo structure.
source: Surprisingly, the backbone residues F576 and G577 forming the TRPC4 selectivity filter show a slightly wider radius in the ligand-bound structures compared to the apo structure.
evidence: This is directly observed by comparing pore radii in different structures.

claim: A density in the selectivity filter of ligand-bound structures indicates that a cation, presumably Ca2+ or Na+, resides in the filter.
source: This could be due to a density in the selectivity filter which we did not observe in the apo structure, indicating that a cation, presumably Ca2+ or Na+, resides in the filter, while the filter is empty in the apo form (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM density maps.

claim: A characteristic lipid density is situated close to the pore in ligand-bound structures, which is either phosphatidic acid or ceramide-1-phosphate.
source: In the ligand-bound structures a characteristic lipid density is situated close to the pore which is either phosphatidic acid or ceramide-1-phosphate, its structural analogue (Vinayagam et al., 2018).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM density and modeled based on the density shape.

claim: The annular lipid co-purified with the protein since no lipids were added during purification.
source: Since we did not add lipids during our purification, this annular lipid likely co-purified with the protein.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental protocol and the presence of lipid density.

claim: The lipid site could be crucial for the gating of the channel, since small molecules can bind in this region and modulate the channel.
source: We hypothesize that this lipid site could be crucial for the gating of the channel, since small molecules can bind in this region, and modulate the channel as observed in activator-bound TRPC6 (Bai et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural observations and comparison with TRPC6.

claim: A putative cation was identified in the Ca2+ binding site of the VSL domain in the ligand-bound structures.
source: We identified density for a putative cation in the Ca2+ binding site of the VSL domain in the ligand-bound structures (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2), also present in the apo structure of TRPC4 (Vinayagam et al., 2018).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM density.

claim: The ion binding site is coordinated by the carbonyl oxygen of D438 and N435 of the S3 helix, along with E417 and Q420 of the S2 helix.
source: The ion binding site is coordinated by the carbonyl oxygen of D438 and N435 of the S3 helix, along with E417 and Q420 of the S2 helix, which are the favorable coordination residues for an alkaline earth metal ion such as Ca2+ (Zheng et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure and supported by citation to Zheng et al., 2017a.

claim: An oxo group of the ligands could complete the octahedral coordination of Ca2+ via a bridging water molecule.
source: Interestingly, not only is a hydroxyl group of Y429 close to the density but also an oxo group of the ligands, which could complete the octahedral coordination of Ca2+ via a bridging water molecule.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural arrangement and coordination geometry.

claim: The presence of the ligands could help to stabilize bound Ca2+.
source: The presence of the ligands could thus help to stabilize bound Ca2+.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations.

claim: TRPC5 and TRPC4 activation has been reported to be Ca2+-dependent.
source: TRPC5 and TRPC4 activation has been reported to be Ca2+-dependent (Plant and Schaefer, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Plant and Schaefer, 2003.

claim: The binding of Ca2+ has been described for TRPM4 and TRPM8, both of which are known to be activated by Ca2+.
source: Similar to our observation here, the binding of Ca2+ has been described for TRPM4 and TRMP8, both of which are also known to be activated by Ca2+.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: The structures of TRPM4 and TRPM8 are in a closed conformation representing the desensitized state.
source: The structures of these channels are in a closed conformation representing the desensitized state (Autzen et al., 2018; Diver et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Autzen et al., 2018; Diver et al., 2019.

claim: CaM has been shown to bind and regulate the TRPC4 channel.
source: CaM has been shown to bind and regulate the TRPC4 channel (Zhu, 2005; Tang et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zhu, 2005; Tang et al., 2001.

claim: At high Ca2+ concentrations in the cytosol, CaM binds in its Ca2+-bound state to TRPC4 and inhibits Ca2+ entry.
source: At high Ca2+ concentrations in the cytosol, CaM binds in its Ca2+-bound state to TRPC4 and inhibits Ca2+ entry.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and citations in the manuscript.

claim: At low Ca2+ concentrations, CaM changes its conformation and dissociates from TRPC4.
source: At low Ca2+ concentrations, CaM changes its conformation and dissociates from the channel.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and citations in the manuscript.

claim: CaM binding to TRPC4 at resting state prevents TRPC4 from being spontaneously activated by IP3 receptors.
source: The store-operated Ca2+ entry pathway hypothesis (Tang et al., 2001) further proposes that CaM binding to the channel at resting state prevents TRPC4 from being spontaneously activated by IP3 receptors.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tang et al., 2001.

claim: TRPC4 was trapped in the CaM column in presence of Ca2+ and released by chelating the Ca2+ with EGTA.
source: As expected, TRPC4 was trapped in the CaM column in presence of Ca2+ and released by chelating the Ca2+ with EGTA (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly supported by pull-down experiment data.

claim: The structure of TRPC4 in LMNG in complex with CaM was determined.
source: We then determined the structure of TRPC4 in LMNG in complex with CaM.
evidence: This is directly supported by cryo-EM data.

claim: The CaM complex sample yielded a 3.3 Å map with applied C4 symmetry.
source: The CaM complex sample yielded a 3.3 Å map with applied C4 symmetry (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is directly supported by cryo-EM data processing.

claim: 13% of the TRPC4 channels had one CaM bound, 35% had two, 31% had three, and 20% were fully saturated with four CaMs.
source: 13% of the TRPC4 channels had one CaM-bound, 35% and 31% had two or three bound, respectively and only 20% were fully saturated (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is directly determined from 3D classification without symmetry.

claim: Four helices corresponding to one lobe of CaM were identified and flexibly fitted.
source: We could clearly identify four helices that correspond to the helices of one lobe of CaM and flexibly fitted this part of the protein (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM density.

claim: The other CaM lobe was not resolved, indicating that this part of the protein is more flexible in this complex.
source: The other CaM lobe was not resolved, indicating that this part of the protein is more flexible in this complex.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of clear density for the second lobe.

claim: CaM binds to the tip of the rib helix (residues 691–703) and the following loop (residues 677–690) that connects the rib helix with a newly identified helix (residues 666–676).
source: Based on the flexibly fitted atomic model we observed that CaM not only binds to the tip of the rib helix (residues 691–703) and the following loop (residues 677–690) that connects the rib helix with a newly identified helix (residues 666–676), but it also interacts with the adjoining loop region comprising residues 273–277 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure.

claim: CaM also interacts with the adjoining loop region comprising residues 273–277 of TRPC4.
source: Based on the flexibly fitted atomic model we observed that CaM not only binds to the tip of the rib helix (residues 691–703) and the following loop (residues 677–690) that connects the rib helix with a newly identified helix (residues 666–676), but it also interacts with the adjoining loop region comprising residues 273–277 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure.

claim: The core region of CaM binds to TRPC4 by forming hydrophobic interactions, while the peripheral residues of CaM are stabilized by hydrophilic interactions.
source: The core region of CaM binds to TRPC4 by forming hydrophobic interactions, while the peripheral residues of CaM are stabilized by hydrophilic interactions (Figure 5D) that are typically observed in CaM-protein/peptide complexes (Villalobo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure and supported by citation to Villalobo et al., 2018.

claim: The interacting residues of TRPC4 with CaM partially overlap with a peptide corresponding to residues 695–724 that have been previously shown to interact with CaM.
source: The interacting residues of TRPC4 partially overlap with a peptide corresponding to residues 695–724 that have been previously shown to interact with CaM (Tang et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with previous studies and citation to Tang et al., 2001.

claim: Residues 695–703 are sufficient for CaM binding in vitro.
source: Since our structure revealed that CaM only interacts with residues 688–703, we conclude that the residues 695–703 are sufficient for CaM binding in vitro.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data.

claim: Residues 704–725 of the rib helix interact with the protein core and are inaccessible for interaction with CaM.
source: Residues 704–725 of the rib helix interact with the protein core and are inaccessible for interaction with CaM.
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure.

claim: The apo structure of TRPC4 in LMNG reached a resolution of 2.85 Å.
source: The apo structure of TRPC4 in LMNG reached a resolution of 2.85 Å, allowing us to build an atomic model with high accuracy (Figure 5—figure supplements 3B, 4).
evidence: This is directly supported by cryo-EM data.

claim: An additional density corresponding to a horizontal helix located at the transmembrane-cytoplasmic interface (residues 666–676) was observed in both the apo and CaM-bound structures.
source: However, in both the apo and CaM-bound structure, we observed for the first time an additional density corresponding to a horizontal helix located at the transmembrane-cytoplasmic interface outside the transmembrane core (residues 666–676) (Figure 5B–D, Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM density.

claim: The horizontal helix has an amphipathic nature with hydrophobic residues facing the transmembrane helix and inner lipid leaflet while hydrophilic residues project into the cytoplasm.
source: The hydrophobic residues of this helix face the transmembrane helix and the inner lipid leaflet while the hydrophilic residues project into the cytoplasm, giving the helix an amphipathic nature.
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure.

claim: Both the apo and CaM-bound TRPC4 structures showed the same constriction of 0.7 Å defined by N621 at the lower gate indicating the closed state of the channel.
source: Both, the apo and CaM-bound TRPC4 structures showed the same constriction of 0.7 Å defined by N621 at the lower gate indicating the closed state of the channel (Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is directly measured from the structures.

claim: When CaM binds to TRPC4 the selectivity filter is slightly widened and contains a density that likely corresponds to Ca2+ or Na+.
source: Interestingly, when CaM binds to TRPC4 the selectivity filter is slightly widened and contains a density that likely corresponds to Ca2+ or Na+ as in the case of the inhibitor-bound channel.
evidence: This is directly observed by comparing the structures.

claim: A much stronger density at the Ca2+ binding site in the VSL domain was observed for the CaM-bound structure compared to apo TRPC4, presumably due to the high Ca2+ concentration used for preparing the CaM-TRPC4 complex.
source: We observed a much stronger density at the Ca2+ binding site in the VSL domain for the CaM-bound structure compared to apo TRPC4, presumably due to the high Ca2+ concentration we used for preparing the CaM-TRPC4 complex.
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM density and inferred from the experimental conditions.

claim: CaM binding stabilizes a longer stretch (residues 677–692) of TRPC4 that is highly flexible in the apo state of the channel.
source: The differences between TRPC4-CaM and the TRPC4 apo structure are more pronounced at the periphery of the channel. There, CaM binding stabilizes a longer stretch (residues 677–692) of TRPC4 that is highly flexible in the apo state of the channel (Figure 5B C).
evidence: This is directly observed by comparing the structures.

claim: Binding of CaM to TRPC4 likely reduces the overall flexibility of the channel, fixing it in its closed state.
source: Therefore, binding of CaM to this region of TRPC4 likely reduces the overall flexibility of the channel, fixing it in its closed state (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations.

claim: One TRPC4 tetramer can bind up to four CaMs.
source: Since one TRPC4 tetramer can bind up to four CaMs, this suggests that the number of CaMs simultaneously bound to TRPC4 could fine tune the level of channel activity.
evidence: This is directly observed from the 3D classification showing different stoichiometries.

claim: The number of CaMs simultaneously bound to TRPC4 could fine tune the level of channel activity.
source: Since one TRPC4 tetramer can bind up to four CaMs, this suggests that the number of CaMs simultaneously bound to TRPC4 could fine tune the level of channel activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of variable stoichiometry.

claim: The mechanism of CaM-mediated regulation of TRPC4 completely differs from that described for TRPV5 and TRPV6.
source: Importantly, this mechanism of CaM-mediated regulation completely differs from that described for other TRP channels, such as TRPV5 and TRPV6 (Hughes et al., 2018; Singh et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is inferred from structural comparison and supported by citations.

claim: In TRPV5 and TRPV6, CaM binds in a 1:4 stoichiometry to the center of the tetrameric channels via the open cytoplasmic part, plugging it with its protruding lysine residue.
source: There, CaM binds in a 1:4 stoichiometry, with one CaM binding to the center of the tetrameric channels via the open cytoplasmic part, plugging it with its protruding lysine residue (Figure 6; Hughes et al., 2018; Singh et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hughes et al., 2018; Singh et al., 2018a.

claim: In the TRPC4-CaM complex structure, the central core of the cytoplasmic region is occupied by a coiled coil helix, preventing CaM from accessing the core.
source: In the TRPC4-CaM complex structure, the central core of the cytoplasmic region is occupied by a coiled coil helix. Thus, CaM cannot access the core of the cytoplasmic region in TRPC4.
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure.

claim: Other channels of the TRPC subfamily also contain the coiled coil helix and the rib helix.
source: Other channels of the TRPC subfamily also contain this coiled coil helix and the rib helix (Duan et al., 2018; Tang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Duan et al., 2018; Tang et al., 2018.

claim: The novel mechanism of CaM inhibition via binding to the rib helix is paradigmatic for all TRPCs.
source: Therefore, we propose that the novel mechanism of CaM inhibition via binding to the rib helix is paradigmatic for all TRPCs.
evidence: This is inferred from structural comparison with other TRPC channels.

claim: The channel switches between its closed and open conformation.
source: In our model, the channel switches between its closed and open conformation as was proposed for many other channels.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of ion channel gating.

claim: Upon binding of an activator, the channel opens transiently and allows the passage of Ca2+.
source: Upon binding of an activator, the channel opens transiently and allows the passage of Ca2+.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge and the proposed model.

claim: Binding of inhibitors locks the channel in its closed conformation and possibly results in a dissociation of the activator.
source: Binding of inhibitors locks the channel in its closed conformation and possibly results in a dissociation of the activator.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data and competition assays.

claim: Subtle conformational changes in the VSL domain appear to be sufficient to transfer the signal from the periphery to the center of the channel to modulate its activity.
source: Thus, subtle conformational changes in this sensitive regulatory domain appear to be sufficient to transfer the signal from the periphery to the center of the channel to modulate its activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations.

claim: High concentrations of the activator can reverse the inhibitory effect.
source: High concentrations of the activator can reverse this effect (Figure 1).
evidence: This is directly supported by the competition assay data in Figure 1.

claim: The rib helix has been shown to be the binding site for the IP3 receptor which acts as an activator of TRPC4.
source: Interestingly, the rib helix has also been shown to be the binding site for the IP3 receptor which acts as an activator of TRPC4 (Tang et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tang et al., 2001.

claim: Inhibition by CaM and activation by IP3 receptor likely use the same binding site on TRPC4, while resulting in opposing effects.
source: Although we do not yet know the structural details of this interaction, it is likely that inhibition by CaM and activation by IP3 receptor require the use the same binding site, while resulting in opposing effects.
evidence: This is inferred from the known binding sites and functional effects.

claim: Activation by DAG likely happens by binding of the secondary messenger to the previously identified lipid binding site close to the channel pore.
source: Activation by DAG (Storch et al., 2017) likely happens by binding of the secondary messenger to the previously identified lipid binding site (Vinayagam et al., 2018) close to the channel pore.
evidence: This is inferred from the location of the lipid binding site and supported by citations.

claim: DAG activation would act directly on the pore region to open the channel.
source: Thus, DAG activation would act directly on the pore region to open the channel.
evidence: This is inferred from the proposed binding site near the pore.

claim: TRPC4 contains several molecular switch regions that can be modulated by the binding of small molecules or regulatory proteins.
source: Thus, TRPC4 contains several molecular switch regions that can be modulated by the binding of small molecules or regulatory proteins (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data showing multiple binding sites.

claim: The signals of different switches are integrated and together determine the final state and the degree of activation of the channel.
source: Consequently, the signals of different switches are integrated and together determine the final state and the degree of activation of the channel.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of multiple regulatory sites.
